tabard.etymology: OE. tabard, tabart; cf. Sp. & Pg. tabardo, It. tabarro, W. tabar, LGr. , LL. tabardum.

tabernacle.etymology: F., fr. L. tabernaculum, dim. of taberna nut. See Tabern.

tableau.etymology: F., dim. fr. L. tabula a painting. See Table.

tablet.etymology: F. tablette, dim. of table. See Table.

tabor.etymology: OF. tabor, tabour, F. tambour; cf. Pr. tabor, tanbor, Sp. & Pg. tambor, atambor, It. tamburo; all fr. Ar. & Per. tamb a kind of lute, or giutar, or Per. tabir a drum. Cf. Tabouret, Tambour.

tabouret.etymology: F., dim. of OF. tabor, tabour, drum. See Tabor.

tabular.etymology: L. tabularis, fr. tabula a board, table. See Table.

tabulate.etymology: L. tabula a table. See Tabular.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.
A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.
A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

tacit.etymology: L. tacitus, p.p. of tacere to be silent, to pass over in silence; akin to Goth. to be silent, Icel. , OHG. dagen: cf. F. tacite. Cf. Reticent.

taciturn.etymology: L. taciturnus: cf. F. taciturne. See Tacit.

tack.etymology: From an old or dialectal form of F. tache. See Techy.

tackle.etymology: OE. takel, akin to LG. & D. takel, Dan. takkel, Sw. tackel; perhaps akin to E. taw, v.t., or to take.

tact.etymology: L. tactus a touching, touch, fr. tangere, tactum, to touch: cf. F. tact. See Tangent.

tactile.etymology: L. tactilis, fr. tangere, tactum, to touch: cf. F. tactile.

tadpole.etymology: OE. tadde toad (AS. tadie, tadige) + poll; properly, a toad that is or seems all head. See Toad, and Poll.

tael.etymology: Malay ta, a certain weight, probably fr. Hind. tola, Skr. tula a balance, weight, tul to weigh.

taffeta.etymology: F. taffetas, It. taffetà, from Per. taftah, originally, twisted, woven, from taftan to twist, to spin.

taffrail.etymology: D. tafereel a panel, picture, fr. tafel table, fr. L. tabula. See Table.

tag.etymology: Probably akin to tack a small nail; cf. Sw. tagg a prickle, point, tooth.

taguan.etymology: From the native name in the East Indies.

tail.etymology: F. taille a cutting. See Entail, Tally.

tailor.etymology: OF. tailleor, F. tailleur, fr. OF. taillier, F. tailler to cut, fr. L. talea a rod, stick, a cutting, layer for planting. Cf. Detail, Entail, Retail, Tally, n.

taint.etymology: Cf. F. atteinte a blow, bit, stroke. See Attaint.

take.etymology: Icel. taka; akin to Sw. taga, Dan. tage, Goth. tekan to touch; of uncertain origin.

talaria.etymology: L., from talaris pertaining to the ankles, fr. talus ankle.

talc.etymology: F. talc; cf. Sp. & It. talco, LL. talcus; all fr. Ar. talq.

tale.etymology: AS. talu number, speech, narrative; akin to D. taal speech, language, G. zahl number, OHG. zala, Icel. tal, tala, number, speech, Sw. tal, Dan. tal number, tale speech, Goth. talzjan to instruct. Cf. Tell, v. t., Toll a tax, also Talk, v. i.

talent.etymology: F., fr. L. talentum a talent (in sense 1), Gr. tolerare, tollere, to lift up, sustain, endure. See Thole, v. t., Tolerate.

talipes.etymology: NL., fr. L. talus an ankle + pes, pedis, a foot; cf. L. talipedare to be weak in the feet, properly, to walk on the ankles.

talipot.etymology: Hind. talpat the leaf of the tree.

talk.etymology: Cf. LG. talk talk, gabble, Prov. G. talken to speak indistinctly; or OD. tolken to interpret, MHG. tolkan to interpret, to tell, to speak indistinctly, Dan. tolke to interpret, Sw. tolka, Icel. t to interpret, t an interpreter, Lith. tulkas an interpreter, tulkanti, tulkoti, to interpret, Russ. tolkovate to interpret, to talk about; or perhaps fr. OE. talien to speak (see Tale, v. i. & n.).

tall.etymology: OE. tal seemly, elegant, docile; of uncertain origin; cf. AS. un-tala, un-tale, bad, Goth. untals indocile, disobedient, uninstructed, or W. & Corn. tal high, Ir. talla meet, fit, proper, just.

tallow.etymology: OE. taluh, talugh; akin to OD. talgh, D. talk, G., Dan. and Sw. talg, Icel. tolgr, tolg, tolk; and perhaps to Goth. tulgus firm.

tally.etymology: OE. taile, taille, F. taille a cutting, cut tally, fr. tailler to cut, but influenced probably by taillé, p.p. of tailler. See Tailor, and cf. Tail a limitation, Taille, Tallage.

talmud.etymology: Chald. talmud instruction, doctrine, fr. lamad to learn, limmad to teach.

talon.etymology: F., heel, spur, LL. talo, fr. L. talus the ankle, heel.

talus.etymology: L., the ankle, the ankle bone.

tamandu.etymology: Sp., from the native name: cf. F. tamandua.

tamarin.etymology: From the native name in Cayenne.

tamarind.etymology: It. tamarindo, or Sp. tamarindo, or Pg. tamarindo, tamarinho, from Ar. tamarhindi, literally, Indian date; tamar a dried date + Hind India: cf. F. tamarin. Cf. Hindoo.

tamarisk.etymology: L. tamariscus, also tamarix, tamarice, Skr. tamala, tamalaka, a tree with a very dark bark; cf. tamas darkness: cf. F. tamarisc, tamarix, tamaris.

tambourine.etymology: F. tambourin; cf. It. tamburino. See Tambour, and cf. Tamborine.

tame.etymology: Cf. F. entamer to cut into, to broach.

tamp.etymology: Cf. F. tamponner to plug or stop. See Tampion.

tampion.etymology: F. tampon, tapon, tape, of Dutch or German origin. See Tap a pipe or plug, and cf. Tamp, Tampop, Tompion.

tanager.etymology: NL. tanagra, probably fr. Brazilian tangara.

tandem.etymology: L. tandem at length (of time only), punningly taken as meaning, lengthwise.

tang.etymology: Of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. tang seaweed, Sw. tång, Icel. þang. Cf. Tangle.

tangent.etymology: L. tangens, -entis, p.pr. of tangere to touch; akin to Gr. tangente. Cf. Attain, Contaminate, Contingent, Entire, Tact, Taste, Tax, v. t.

tangible.etymology: L. tangibilis, fr. tangere to touch: cf. F. tangible. See Tangent.

tangle.etymology: A frequentative fr. tang seaweed; hence, to twist like seaweed. See Tang seaweed, and cf. Tangle, n.

tank.etymology: Pg. tanque, L. stangum a pool; or perhaps of East Indian origin. Cf. Stank, n.

tankard.etymology: OF. tanquart; cf. OD. tanckaert; of uncertain origin.

tansy.etymology: OE. tansaye, F. tanaise; cf. It. & Sp. tanaceto, NL. tanacetum, Pg. atanasia, athanasia, Gr. 'aqanasi`a immortality, fr. 'aqa`natos immortal; 'a priv. + qa`natos death.

tantalum.etymology: NL. So named on account of the perplexity and difficulty encounterd by its discoverer (Ekeberg) in isolating it. See Tantalus.

tantamount.etymology: F. tant so much (L. tantus) + E. amount.

tap.etymology: F. taper to strike; of Teutonic origin; cf. dial. G. tapp, tapps, a blow, tappe a paw, fist, G. tappen to grope.

tape.etymology: AS. tæppe a fillet. Cf. Tapestry, Tippet.

taper.etymology: AS. tapur, tapor, taper; cf. Ir. tapar, W. tampr.

tapestry.etymology: F. tapissere, fr. tapisser to carpet, to hang, or cover with tapestry, fr. tapis a carpet, carpeting, LL. tapecius, fr. L. tapete carpet, tapestry, Gr. Tapis, Tippet.

tapioca.etymology: Braz. tapioka: cf. Pg., Sp. & F. tapioca.

tapster.etymology: AS. tæppestre a female tapster. See Tap a plug, pipe, and -ster.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the agent (originally a woman), especially a person who does something with skill or as an occupation; as in spinster (originally, a woman who spins), songster, baxter (= bakester), youngster.

tarantism.etymology: It. tarantismo: cf. F. tarentisme. See Tarantula.

tarantula.etymology: NL., fr. It. tarantola, fr. L. Tarentum, now Taranto, in the south of Italy.

tarboosh.etymology: Ar. tarb; perhaps from Per. sar-posh headdress: cf. F. tarbouch.

tardigrade.etymology: L. tardigradus; tardus slow + gradi to step: cf. F. tardigrade.

tardy.etymology: F. tardif, fr. (assumed) LL. tardivus, fr. L. tardus slow.

tare.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. tare brisk, eager, OE. tarefitch the wild vetch.

target.etymology: OF. targette, dim. of OF. & F. targe, of Teutonic origin; cf. AS. targe, OD. targie, G. zarge a frame, case, border, OHG. zarga, Icel. targa shield.

tariff.etymology: F. tarif; cf. Sp. & Pg. tarifa, It. tariffa; all fr. Ar. ta'rif information, explanation, definition, from 'arafa, to know, to inform, explain.

tarnish.etymology: F. ternir, fr. OHG. tarnen to darken, to conceal, hide; akin to OS. dernian to hide, AS. dernan, dyrnan, OHG. tarni hidden, OS. derni, AS. derne, dyrne. Cf. Dern, a., and see -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

tarpaulin.etymology: Tar + palling a covering, pall to cover. See Pall a covering.

tarragon.etymology: Sp. taragona, Ar. tarkh; perhaps fr. Gr. draco; cf. L. dracunculus tarragon. Cf. Dragon.

tart.etymology: AS. teart. *63. Cf. Tear, v. t.

tartan.etymology: F. tiretane linsey-woolsey, akin to Sp. tiritaña a sort of thin silk; cf. Sp. tiritar to shiver or shake with cold.

task.etymology: OE. taske, OF. tasque, F. tâche, for tasche, LL. tasca, taxa, fr. L. taxare to rate, appraise, estimate. See Tax, n. & v.

taste.etymology: OE. tasten to feel, to taste, OF. taster, F. tater to feel, to try by the touch, to try, to taste, (assumed) LL. taxitare, fr. L. taxare to touch sharply, to estimate. See Tax, v. t.

tatouay.etymology: Of Brazilian origin; cf. Pg. tatu, F. tatou.

tatter.etymology: Icel. tötur, töttur, pl. tötrar, ; cf. Norw. totra, pl. totror, LG. taltern tatters. *240.

tatterdemalion.etymology: Tatter + OF. desmaillier to break the meshes of, to tear: cf. OF. maillon long clothes, swadding clothes, F. maillot. See Tatter, and Mail armor.

tattle.etymology: Akin to OE. tateren, LG. tateln, D. tateren to stammer, and perhaps to E. titter.

tattoo.etymology: Earlier taptoo, D. taptoe; tap a tap, faucet + toe to, shut (i. e., the taps, or drinking houses, shut from the soldiers).

tau.etymology: Gr. tay^ the letter t (English T).

taunt.etymology: Cf. OF. tant so great, F. tant so much, L. tantus of such size, so great, so much.

taurine.etymology: L. taurinus, fr. taurus a bull. See Taurus.

taurus.etymology: L., akin to Gr. steer. See Steer a young ox.

taut.etymology: Dan. tæt; akin to E. tight. See Tight.

tautog.etymology: The pl. of taut, the American Indian name, translated by Roger Williams sheep's heads, and written by him tautaúog.

tavern.etymology: OE. taverne, F. taverne, from L. taberna a hut, booth, tavern. Cf. Table, Tabernacle.

taw.etymology: Cf. Tew to tow, Tow, v. t.

tawdry.etymology: Said to be corrupted from Saint Audrey, or Auldrey, meaning Saint Ethelreda, implying therefore, originally, bought at the fair of St. Audrey, where laces and gay toys of all sorts were sold. This fair was held in Isle Ely, and probably at other places, on the day of the saint, which was the 17th of October.

tawny.etymology: F. tanné, p.p. of tanner to tan. See Tan, v. t. & n. Cf. Tenné.

tax.etymology: F. taxe, fr. taxer to tax, L. taxare to touch, sharply, to feel, handle, to censure, value, estimate, fr. tangere, tactum, to touch. See Tangent, and cf. Task, Taste.

taxation.etymology: F. taxation, L. taxatio a valuing, estimation, from L. taxare. See Tax.

taxidermy.etymology: Gr. taxidermie. See Tactics, Tear, v. t.

tea.etymology: Chin. tsha, Prov. Chin. te: cf. F. thé.

teach.etymology: OE. techen, imp. taughte, tahte, AS. t, imp. t, to show, teach, akin to tacn token. See Token.

teal.etymology: OE. tele; akin to D. teling a generation, production, teal, telen to breed, produce, and E. till to cultivate. The English word probably once meant, a brood or flock. See Till to cultivate.

team.etymology: OE. tem, team, AS. teám, offspring, progeny, race of descendants, family; akin to D. toom a bridle, LG. toom progeny, team, bridle, G. zaum a bridle, zeugen to beget, Icel. taumr to rein, bridle, Dan. tömme, Sw. töm, and also to E. tow to drag, tug to draw. *64. See Tug, and cf. Teem to bear.

tear.etymology: AS. teár; akin to G. zärhe, OHG. zahar, OFries. & Icel. tar, Sw. tår, Dan. taare, Goth. tagr, OIr. der, W. dagr, OW. dacr, L. lacrima, lacruma, for older dacruma, Gr. Lachrymose.

tease.etymology: AS. t to pluck, tease; akin to OD. teesen, MHG. zeisen, Dan. tæse, tæsse. *58. Cf. Touse.

teasel.etymology: OE. tesel, AS. t, t, the fuller's herb. See Tease.

teat.etymology: OE. tete, titte, AS. tit, titt; akin to LG. & OD. titte, D. tet, G. zitze: cf. F. tette, probably of Teutonic origin.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

techy.etymology: From OE. tecche, tache, a habit, bad habit, vice, OF. tache, teche, a spot, stain, blemish, habit, vice, F. tache a spot, blemish; probably akin to E. tack a small nail. See Tack a small nail, and cf. Touchy.

ted.etymology: Prob. fr. Icel. te to spread manure, fr. ta manure; akin to MHG. zetten to scatter, spread. *58. Cf. Teathe.

tedious.etymology: L. taediosus, fr. taedium. See Tedium.

tedium.etymology: L. taedium, fr. taedet it disgusts, it wearies one.

tee.etymology: Cf. Icel. tja to show, mark.

teem.etymology: Icel. tæma to empty, from tomr empty; akin to Dan. tömme to empty, Sw. tömma. See Toom to empty.

teen.etymology: OE. tene, AS. teóna reproach, wrong, fr. teón to accuse; akin to G. zeihen, Goth. gateihan to tell, announce, L. dicere to say. See Token.

teeter.etymology: Prov. E. titter to tremble, to seesaw; cf. Icel. titra to tremble, OHG. zittaron, G. zittern.

teetotum.etymology: For T-totum. It was used for playing games of chance, and was four-sided, one side having the letter T on it, standing for Latin totum all, meaning, take all that is staked, whence the name. The other three sides each had a letter indicating an English or Latin word; as P meaning put down, N nothing or L. nil, H half. See Total.

tegular.etymology: LL. tegularis, from L. tegula a tile. See Tile.

tegument.etymology: L. tegumentum, from tegere to cover. See Thatch, n., and cf. Detect, Protect.

roots.meaning: A suffix indicating something drawn or written, a drawing, writing; -- as, monogram, telegram, chronogram.

telegraph.etymology: Gr. toli) + -graph: cf. F. télégraphe. See Graphic.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

teleology.etymology: Gr. teleos, the end or issue + -logy: cf. F. téléologie.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

tell.etymology: AS. tellan, from talu tale, number, speech; akin to D. tellen to count, G. zählen, OHG. zellen to count, tell, say, Icel. telja, Dan. tale to speak, tælle to count. See Tale that which is told.

telluric.etymology: L. tellus, -uris, the earth: cf. F. tellurique.

tellurium.etymology: NL., from L. tellus, -uris, the earth.

temerity.etymology: L. temeritas, from temere by chance, rashly; perhaps akin to Skr. tamas darkness: cf. F. témérité.

temper.etymology: AS. temprian or OF. temper, F. tempérer, and (in sense 3) temper, L. temperare, akin to tempus time. Cf. Temporal, Distemper, Tamper.

temperament.etymology: L. temperamentum a mixing in due proportion, proper measure, temperament: cf. F. tempérament. See Temper, v. t.

temperance.etymology: L. temperantia: cf. F. tempérance. See Temper, v. t.

temperate.etymology: L. temperatus, p.p. of temperare. See Temper, v. t.

temperature.etymology: F. température, L. temperatura due measure, proportion, temper, temperament.

tempest.etymology: OF. tempeste, F. tempête, (assumed) LL. tempesta, fr. L. tempestas a portion of time, a season, weather, storm, akin to tempus time. See Temporal of time.

tempestuous.etymology: L. tempestuous: cf. OF. tempestueux, F. tempêtueux.

templar.etymology: OE. templere, F. templier, LL. templarius. See Temple a church.

templet.etymology: LL. templatus vaulted, from L. templum a small timber.

tempo.etymology: It., fr. L. tempus. See Tense, n.

temporal.etymology: L. temporalis, fr. tempora the temples: cf. F. temporal. See Temple a part of the head.

temporality.etymology: L. temporalitas, in LL., possessions of the church: cf. F. temporalité.

temporary.etymology: L. temporarius, fr. tempus, temporis, time: cf. F. temporaire.

temporize.etymology: F. temporiser. See Temporal of time.

tempt.etymology: OE. tempten, tenten, from OF. tempter, tenter, F. tenter, fr. L. tentare, temptare, to handle, feel, attack, to try, put to the test, urge, freq. from tendere, tentum, and tensum, to stretch. See Thin, and cf. Attempt, Tend, Taunt, Tent a pavilion, Tent to probe.

temptation.etymology: OF. temptation, tentation, F. tentation, L. tentatio.

ten.etymology: AS. ten, tién, t, tene; akin to OFries. tian, OS. tehan, D. tien, G. zehn, OHG. zehan, Icel. tiu, Sw. tio, Dan. ti, Goth. taíhun, Lith. deszimt, Russ. desiate, W. deg, Ir. & Gael. deich, L. decem, Gr. daçan. *308. Cf. Dean, Decade, Decimal, December, Eighteen, Eighty, Teens, Tithe.

tenable.etymology: F. tenable, fr. tenir to hold, L. tenere. See Thin, and cf. Continue, Continent, Entertain, Maintain, Tenant, Tent.

tenacious.etymology: L. tenax, -acis, from tenere to hold. See Tenable, and cf. Tenace.

tenacity.etymology: L. tenacitas: cf. F. ténacité. See Tenacious.

tenancy.etymology: Cf. OF. tenace, LL. tenentia. See Tenant.

tenant.etymology: F. tenant, p.pr. of tenir to hold. See Tenable, and cf. Lieutenant.

tench.etymology: OF. tenche, F. tanche, L. tinca.

tendency.etymology: L. tendents, -entis, p.pr. of tendere: cf. F. tendance. See Tend to move.

tender.etymology: From Tend to attend. Cf. Attender.

tendon.etymology: F., fr. L. tendere to stretch, extend. See Tend to move.

tendril.etymology: Shortened fr. OF. tendrillon, fr. F. tendre tender; hence, properly, the tender branch or spring of a plant: cf. F. tendrille. See Tender, a., and cf. Tendron.

tenebrific.etymology: L. tenebrae darkness + facere to make.

tenebrous.etymology: L. tenebrosus, fr. tenebrae darkness: cf. F. ténébreux.

tenement.etymology: OF. tenement a holding, a fief, F. tènement, LL. tenementum, fr. L. tenere to hold. See Tenant.

tenet.etymology: L. tenet he holds, fr. tenere to hold. See Tenable.

tennis.etymology: OE. tennes, tenies, tenyse; of uncertain origin, perhaps fr. F. tenez hold or take it, fr. tenir to hold (see Tenable).

tenon.etymology: F., fr. tenir to hold. See Tenable.

tenor.etymology: L., from tenere to hold; hence, properly, a holding on in a continued course: cf. F. teneur. See Tenable, and cf. Tenor a kind of voice.

tenrec.etymology: From the native name: cf. F. tanrac, tanrec, tandrec.

tense.etymology: OF. tens, properly, time, F. temps time, tense. See Temporal of time, and cf. Thing.

tension.etymology: L. tensio, from tendere, tensum, to stretch: cf. F. tension. See Tense, a.

tent.etymology: Sp. tinto, properly, deep-colored, fr. L. tinctus, p.p. of tingere to dye. See Tinge, and cf. Tint, Tinto.

tentacle.etymology: NL. tentaculum, from L. tentare to handle, feel: cf. F. tentacule. See Tempt.

tentative.etymology: L. tentare to try: cf. F. tentatif. See Tempt.

tenter.etymology: OE. tenture, tentoure, OF. tenture a stretching, spreading, F. tenture hangings, tapestry, from L. tendere, tentum, to stretch. See Tend to move.

tenth.etymology: From Ten: cf. OE. tethe, AS. teó. See Ten, and cf. Tithe.

tenuity.etymology: L. tenuitas, from tenuis thin: cf. F. ténuité. See Tenuous.

tenuous.etymology: L. tenuis thin. See Thin, and cf. Tenuis.

tenure.etymology: F. tenure, OF. teneure, fr. F. tenir to hold. See Tenable.

tepal.etymology: F. tépale, fr. pétale, by transposition.

tepid.etymology: L. tepidus, fr. tepere to be warm; akin to Skr. tap to be warm, tapas heat.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

terbium.etymology: NL., fr. Ytterby, in Sweden. See Erbium.

tercet.etymology: F., fr. It. terzetto, dim. of terzo, third, L. tertius. See Tierce, and cf. Terzetto.

terebinth.etymology: L. terbinthus, Gr. térébinthe. Cf. Turpentine.

teredo.etymology: L., a worm that gnaws wood, clothes, etc.; akin to Gr. terere to rub.

terete.etymology: L. teres, -etis, rounded off, properly, rubbed off, fr. terere to rub.

tergiversate.etymology: L. tergiversatus, p.p. of tergiversari to turn one's back, to shift; tergum back + versare, freq. of vertere to turn. See Verse.

term.etymology: F. terme, L. termen, -inis, terminus, a boundary limit, end; akin to Gr. Thrum a tuft, and cf. Terminus, Determine, Exterminate.

termagant.etymology: OE. Trivigant, Termagant, Termagant (in sense 1), OF. Tervagan; cf. It. Trivigante.

termes.etymology: L. termes, tarmes, -itis, a woodworm. Cf. Termite.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

terminal.etymology: L. terminals: cf. F. terminal. See Term, n.

terminate.etymology: L. terminatus, p.p. of terminare. See Term.

termination.etymology: L. terminatio a bounding, fixing, determining: cf. F. terminasion, OF. also termination. See Term.

terminator.etymology: L., he who limits or sets bounds.

terminology.etymology: L. terminus term + -logy: cf. F. terminologie.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

tern.etymology: Dan. terne, tærne; akin to Sw. tärna, Icel. ; cf. NL. sterna.

ternary.etymology: L. ternarius, fr. terni. See Tern, a.

ternate.etymology: NL. ternatus, fr. L. terni three each. See Tern, a.

ternion.etymology: L. ternio, fr. terni three each. See Tern, a.

terrace.etymology: F. terrasse (cf. Sp. terraza, It. terrazza), fr. L. terra the earth, probably for tersa, originally meaning, dry land, and akin to torrere to parch, E. torrid, and thirst. See Thirst, and cf. Fumitory, Inter, v., Patterre, Terrier, Trass, Tureen, Turmeric.

terrene.etymology: L. terrenus, fr. terra the earth. See Terrace.

terreplein.etymology: F., fr. L. terra earth + planus even, level, plain.

terrestrial.etymology: L. terrestris, from terra the earth. See Terrace.

terrible.etymology: F., fr. L. terribilis, fr. terrere to frighten. See Terror.

terrier.etymology: CF. L. terere to rub, to rub away, terebra a borer.

terrific.etymology: L. terrificus; fr. terrere to frighten + facere to make. See Terror, and Fact.

terrify.etymology: L. terrere to frighten + -fy: cf. F. terrifier, L. terrificare. See Terrific, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

territory.etymology: L. territorium, from terra the earth: cf. F. territoire. See Terrace.

terror.etymology: L. terror, akin to terrere to frighten, for tersere; akin to Gr. tras to tremble, to be afraid, Russ. triasti to shake: cf. F. terreur. Cf. Deter.

terse.etymology: L. tersus, p.p. of tergere to rub or wipe off.

tertian.etymology: L. tertianus, from tertius the third. See Tierce.

tertiary.etymology: L. tertiarius containing a third part, fr. tertius third: cf. F. tertiaire. See Tierce.

terzetto.etymology: It., dim. of terzo the third, L. tertius. See Tierce.

tessera.etymology: L., a square piece, a die. See Tessellar.

test.etymology: OE. test test, or cupel, potsherd, F. têt, from L. testum an earthen vessel; akin to testa a piece of burned clay, an earthen pot, a potsherd, perhaps for tersta, and akin to torrere to patch, terra earth (cf. Thirst, and Terrace), but cf. Zend tasta cup. Cf. Test a shell, Testaceous, Tester a covering, a coin, Testy, Tête- à-tête.

testa.etymology: L. testa a piece of burned clay, a broken piece of earthenware, a shell. See Test a cupel.

testacea.etymology: NL., fr. L. testaceum a shelled anumal. See Testaceous.

testaceous.etymology: L. testaceus, fr. testa a shell. See Testa.

testament.etymology: F., fr. L. testamentum, fr. testari to be a witness, to make one's last will, akin to testis a witness. Cf. Intestate, Testify.

testate.etymology: L. testatus, p.p. of testari. See Testament.

tester.etymology: OE. testere a headpiece, helmet, OF. testiere, F. têtière a head covering, fr. OF. teste the head, F. tête, fr. L. testa an earthen pot, the skull. See Test a cupel, and cf. Testière.

testicle.etymology: L. testiculus, dim. of testis a testicle, probably the same word as testis a witness, as being a witness to manhood. Cf. Test a witness.

testiere.etymology: OF. testiere. See Tester a headpiece.

testify.etymology: OF. testifier, L. testificari; testis a witness + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy, and cf. Attest, Contest, Detest, Protest, Testament.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

testimonial.etymology: Cf. OF. testimoniale, LL. testimonialis, L. testimoniales (sc. litteræ). See Testimonial, a.

testimony.etymology: L. testimonium, from testis a witness: cf. OF. testimoine, testemoine, testimonie. See Testify.

testudo.etymology: L., from testa the shell of shellfish, or of testaceous animals.

testy.etymology: OF. testu obstinate, headstrong, F. têtu, fr. OF. teste the head, F. tête. See Test a cupel.

tetanic.etymology: Cf. L. tetanicus suffering from tetanus, Gr. tétanique.

tether.etymology: Formerly tedder, OE. tedir; akin to LG. tider, tier, Icel. tjo, Dan. töir. *64.

teuton.etymology: L. Teutones, Teutoni, the name of a Germanic people, probably akin to E. Dutch. Cf. Dutch.

teutonic.etymology: L. Teutonicus, from Teutoni, or Teutones. See Teuton.

text.etymology: F. texte, L. textus, texture, structure, context, fr. texere, textum, to weave, construct, compose; cf. Gr. taksh to cut, carve, make. Cf. Context, Mantle, n., Pretext, Tissue, Toil a snare.

textile.etymology: L. textilis, fr. texere to weave: cf. F. textile. See Text.

texture.etymology: L. textura, fr. texere, textum, to weave: cf. F. texture. See Text.

thallium.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. green line in its spectrum.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

thane.etymology: OE. thein, Þein, AS. Þegen, Þegn; akin to OHG. degan a follower, warrior, boy, MHG. degen a hero, G. degen hero, soldier, Icel. Þegn a thane, a freeman; probably akin to Gr. Þius servant, AS. Þeón, G. dienen to serve.

thank.etymology: AS. Þanc, Þonc, thanks, favor, thought; akin to OS. thank favor, pleasure, thanks, D. & G. dank thanks, Icel. Þ\'94kk, Dan. tak, Sw. tack, Goth. Þagks thanks; -- originally, a thought, a thinking. See Think.

thatch.etymology: OE. thak, AS. Þ\'91c a roof; akin to Þeccean to cover, D. dak a roof, dekken to cover, G. dach a roof, decken 8cover, Icel. Þak a roof, Sw. tak, Dan. tag, Lith. stogas, Ir. teagh a house, Gael. teach, tigh, W. ty, L. tegere to cover, toga a toga, Gr. sthag. Cf. Deck, Integument, Tile, Toga.

theater.etymology: F. thé\'83tre, L. theatrum, Gr. dhya to meditate, think. Cf. Theory.

theatre.etymology: F. thé\'83tre, L. theatrum, Gr. dhya to meditate, think. Cf. Theory.

theca.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Tick a cover.

theft.etymology: OE. thefte, AS. Þiéfthe, Þ\'dffthe, Þeófthe. See Thief.

their.etymology: From Old Norse þeira , þeirra . Replaced native Old English heora .

theism.etymology: From Gr. théisme. Cf. Enthusiasm, Pantheon, Theology.

theme.etymology: OE. teme, OF. teme, F. thème, L. thema, Gr. Do, and cf. Thesis.

then.etymology: Originally the same word as than. See Than.

thence.etymology: OE. thenne, thanne, and (with the adverbal -s; see -wards) thennes, thannes (hence thens, now written thence), AS. thanon, thanan, thonan; akin to OHG. dannana, dannan, danan, and G. von dannen, E. that, there. See That.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

theocracy.etymology: Gr. théocratie. See Theism, and cf. Democracy.

theodolite.etymology: Probably a corruption of the alidade. See Alidade.

theogony.etymology: L. theogonia, Gr. Theism, and Genus.

theologian.etymology: Cf. F. théologien, L. theologus, Gr. Theology.

theology.etymology: L. theologia, Gr. théologie. See Theism, and Logic.

theorem.etymology: L. theorema, Gr. théorème. See Theory.

theory.etymology: F. théorie, L. theoria, Gr. Theater.

there.etymology: OE. ther, AS. th\'d6r; akin to D. daar, G. da, OHG. dar, Sw. & Dan. der, Icel. & Goth. Þar, Skr. tarhi then, and E. that. *184. See That, pron.

thereabout.etymology: The latter spelling is less proper, but more commonly used.

thereabouts.etymology: The latter spelling is less proper, but more commonly used.

thereafter.etymology: AS. th\'d6ræfter after that. See There, and After.

therefore.etymology: OE. therfore. See There, and Fore, adv., For, and cf. Therefor.

thermal.etymology: L. thermae hot springs, fr. Gr. formus warm, and E. forceps.

thermometer.etymology: Thermo- + -meter: cf. F. thermomètre. See Thermal.

thesis.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Do, and cf. Anathema, Apothecary, Epithet, Hypothesis, Parenthesis, Theme, Tick a cover.

theurgy.etymology: L. theurgia, Gr. théurgie. See Theism, and Work.

thick.etymology: OE. thicke, AS. ; akin to D. dik, OS. thikki, OHG. dicchi thick, dense, G. dick thick, Icel. , , and probably to Gael. & Ir. tiugh. Cf. Tight.

thief.etymology: OE. thef, theef, AS. ; akin to OFries. thiaf, OS. theof, thiof, D. dief, G. dieb, OHG. diob, Icel. , Sw. tjuf, Dan. tyv, Goth. , , and perhaps to Lith. tupeti to squat or crouch down. Cf. Theft.

thigh.etymology: OE. thi, , , AS. ; akin to OFries. thiach, D. dij, dije, OHG. dioh, thioh, Icel. thigh, rump, and probably to Lith. taukas fat of animals, tuk to become fat, Russ. tuke fat of animals. *56.

thill.etymology: OE. thille, AS. a board, plank, beam, thill; akin to a plank, D. deel a plank, floor, G. diele, OHG. dili, dilla, Icel. a plank, planking, a thwart, a wainscot, plank; cf. Skr. tala a level surface. *236. Cf. Fill a thill, Deal a plank.

thimble.etymology: OE. thimbil, AS. , fr. a thumb. *56. See Thumb.

thin.etymology: OE. thinne, thenne, thunne, AS. þynne; akin to D. dun, G. dünn, OHG. dunni, Icel. þunnr, Sw. tunn, Dan. tynd, Gael. & Ir. tana, W. teneu, L. tenuis, Gr. tanu thin, slender; also to AS. to extend, G. dehnen, Icel. , Goth. (in comp.), L. tendere to stretch, tenere to hold, Gr. tan. *51 & 237. Cf. Attenuate, Dance, Tempt, Tenable, Tend to move, Tenous, Thunder, Tone.

thing.etymology: AS. þing a thing, cause, assembly, judicial assembly; akin to þingan to negotiate, þingian to reconcile, conciliate, D. ding a thing, OS. thing thing, assembly, judicial assembly, G. ding a thing, formerly also, an assembly, court, Icel. þing a thing, assembly, court, Sw. & Dan. ting; perhaps originally used of the transaction of or before a popular assembly, or the time appointed for such an assembly; cf. G. dingen to bargain, hire, MHG. dingen to hold court, speak before a court, negotiate, Goth. þeihs time, perhaps akin to L. tempus time. Cf. Hustings, and Temporal of time.

think.etymology: OE. thinken, properly, to seem, from AS. þyncean (cf. Methinks), but confounded with OE. thenken to think, fr. AS. þencean (imp. þohte); akin to D. denken, dunken, OS. thenkian, thunkian, G. denken, dünken, Icel. þekkja to perceive, to know, þykkja to seem, Goth. þagkjan, þaggkjan, to think, þygkjan to think, to seem, OL. tongere to know. Cf. Thank, Thought.

third.etymology: OE. thirde, AS. , fr. , , three; akin to D. derde third, G. dritte, Icel. , Goth. , L. tertius, Gr. t. See Three, and cf. Riding a jurisdiction, Tierce.

thirst.etymology: OE. thirst, þurst, AS. þurst, þyrst; akin to D. dorst, OS. thurst, G. durst, Icel. þorsti, Sw. & Dan. törst, Goth. þaúrstei thirst, þaúrsus dry, withered, þaúrsieþ mik I thirst, gaþaírsan to wither, L. torrere to parch, Gr. te`rsesqai to become dry, tesai`nein to dry up, Skr. trssh to thirst. *54. Cf. Torrid.

thirteen.etymology: OE. threttene, AS. , . See Three, and Ten, and cf. Thirty.

thirty.etymology: OE. thritty, AS. Þritig, Þrittig; akin to D. dertig, G. dreissig, Icel. Þrjatiu, Þrjatigi, Þrir teger, Goth. Þreis tigjus, i.e., three tens. See Three, and Ten, and cf. Thirteen.

thistle.etymology: OE. thistil, AS. þistel; akin to D. & G. distel, OHG. distila, distil, Icel. þistill, Sw. tistel, Dan. tidsel; of uncertain origin.

thither.etymology: OE. thider, AS. edhider; akin to E. that; cf. Icel. þaedhra there, Goth. þaþro thence. See That, and The.

thole.etymology: OE. thol, AS. þol; akin to D. dol, Icel. þollr a fir tree, a young fir, a tree, a thole.

thong.etymology: OE. thong, þwong, thwang, AS. þwang; akin to Icel. þvengr a thong, latchet. *57. Cf. Twinge.

thorite.etymology: So called by Berzelius from the Scandinavian god Thor. See Thor.

thorn.etymology: AS. þorn; akin to OS. & OFries. thorn, D. doorn, G. dorn, Dan. torn, Sw. törne, Icel. þorn, Goth. þaúrnus; cf. Pol. tarn, Russ. tern' the blackthorn, ternie thorns, Skr. trsnsa grass, blade of grass. *53.

thorpe.etymology: AS. þorp; akin to OS. & OFries. thorp, D. dorp, G. dorf, Icel. þorp, Dan. torp, Sw. torp a cottage, a little farm, Goth. þaúrp a field, and probably to Lith. troba a building, a house, W. tref a hamlet, Ir. treabh a farmed village, a tribe, clan, Gael. treabhair houses, and perhaps to L. turba a crowd, mult. Cf. Dorp.

thou.etymology: OE. thou, þu, AS. edhu, edhu; akin to OS. & OFries. thu, G., Dan. & Sw. du, Icel. þu, Goth. þu, Russ. tui, Ir. & Gael. tu, W. ti, L. tu, Gr. sy`, Dor. ty`, Skr. tvam. *185. Cf. Thee, Thine, Te Deum.

though.etymology: OE. thogh, þah, AS. edheáh, edhæh, edheh; akin to OS. thoh, OFries. thach, D. & G. doch but, yet, OHG. doh but, yet though, Icel. þo yet, nevertheless, Sw. dock, Dan. dog, Goth. þáuh, þáu, than, or, yet; of uncertain origin. *184.

thought.etymology: OE. þoght, þouht, AS. þoht, geþoht, fr. þencean to think; akin to D. gedachte thought, MHG. daht, gedaht, Icel. þottr, þotti. See Think.

thousand.etymology: OE. þousend, þusend, AS. þusend; akin to OS. thusundig, thusind, OFries. thusend, D. duizend, G. tausend, OHG. t, d, Icel. þusund, þushund, Sw. tusen, Dan. tusind, Goth. þusundi, Lith. tukstantis, Russ. tuisiacha; of uncertain origin.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting: (a) Jurisdiction or property and jurisdiction, dominion, as in kingdom earldom. (b) State, condition, or quality of being, as in wisdom, freedom.

thrall.etymology: OE. thral, , Icel. , perhaps through AS. ; akin to Sw. träl, Dan. træl, and probably to AS. to run, Goth. , Gr. dregil, drigil, a servant.

thrash.etymology: OE. , , to beat, AS. , ; akin to D. dorschen, OD. derschen, G. dreschen, OHG. dreskan, Icel. , Sw. tröska, Dan. tærske, Goth. , Lith. traszketi to rattle, Russ. treskate to burst, crackle, tresk' a crash, OSlav. troska a stroke of lighting. Cf. Thresh.

thread.etymology: OE. threed, , AS. ; akin to D. draad, G. draht wire, thread, OHG. drat, Icel. a thread, Sw. tråd, Dan. traad, and AS. to twist. See Throw, and cf. Third.

threat.etymology: AS. , akin to a to vex, G. verdriessen, OHG. irdriozan, Icel. to fail, want, lack, Goth. us to vex, to trouble, Russ. trudite to impose a task, irritate, vex, L. trudere to push. Cf. Abstruse, Intrude, Obstrude, Protrude.

three.etymology: OE. þre, þreo, þri, AS. þri, masc., þreó, fem. and neut.; akin to OFries. thre, OS. thria, threa, D. drie, G. drei, OHG. dri, Icel. þrir, Dan. & Sw. tre, Goth. þreis, Lith. trys, Ir., Gael. & W. tri, Russ. tri, L. tres, Gr. trei^s, Skr. tri. *301. Cf. 3d Drilling, Tern, a., Third, Thirteen, Thirty, Tierce, Trey, Tri-, Triad, Trinity, Tripod.

roots.meaning: A prefix (also used adjectively) denoting three proportional or combining part, or the third degree of that to the name of which it is prefixed; as in trisulphide, trioxide, trichloride.

thresh.etymology: OE. , , to beat, AS. , ; akin to D. dorschen, OD. derschen, G. dreschen, OHG. dreskan, Icel. , Sw. tröska, Dan. tærske, Goth. , Lith. traszketi to rattle, Russ. treskate to burst, crackle, tresk' a crash, OSlav. troska a stroke of lighting. Cf. Thresh.

threshold.etymology: OE. threswold, þreshwold, AS. þrescwald, þerscwald, þerscold, þrescold, fr. þrescan, þerscan, to thresh; akin to Icel. þreskjöde, þröskuldr, Sw. tröskel, Dan. tærskel. See Thrash.

thrice.etymology: OE. thries; thrie thrice (AS. , ) + -s, the adverbal suffix. See Three, and -wards.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

thrive.etymology: OE. , Icel. ; probably originally, to grasp for one's self, from to grasp; akin to Dan. trives to thrive, Sw. trifvas. Cf. Thrift.

throat.etymology: OE. throte, AS. , ; akin to OHG. drozza, G. drossel; cf. OFries. & D. stort. Cf. Throttle.

throb.etymology: OE. ; of uncertain origin; cf. Russ. trepete a trembling, and E. trepidation.

throe.etymology: OE. , , AS. a threatening, oppression, suffering, perhaps influenced by Icel. a throe, a pang, a longing; cf. AS. to suffer.

throne.etymology: OE. trone, F. trône, L. thronus, Gr. dharansa supporting, dhrs to hold fast, carry, and E. firm, a.

throng.etymology: OE. þrong, þrang, AS. geþrang, fr. þringan to crowd, to press; akin to OS. thringan, D. & G. dringen, OHG. dringan, Icel. þryngva, þröngva, Goth. þriehan, D. & G. drang a throng, press, Icel. þröng a throng, Lith. trenkti to jolt, tranksmas a tumult. Cf. Thring.

throstle.etymology: OE. throsel, AS. , ; akin to MHG. trostel, G. drossel, Icel. , Sw. trast, Lith. strazdas, L. turdus. *238. Cf. Thrush the bird.

through.etymology: OE. thurgh, , , , AS. ; akin to OS. thurh, thuru, OFries. thruch, D. door, OHG. durh, duruh, G. durch, Goth. ; cf. Ir. tri, tre, W. trwy. *53. Cf. Nostril, Thorough, Thrill.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the agent (originally a woman), especially a person who does something with skill or as an occupation; as in spinster (originally, a woman who spins), songster, baxter (= bakester), youngster.

thrum.etymology: OE. thrum, throm; akin to OD. drom, D. dreum, G. trumm, lump, end, fragment, OHG. drum end, Icel. edge, brim, and L. terminus a limit, term. Cf. Term.

thrush.etymology: OE. þrusche, AS. þrysce; akin to OHG. drosca, droscea, droscela, and E. throstle. Cf. Throstle.

thrust.etymology: OE. , , , Icel. to thrust, press, force, compel; perhaps akin to E. threat.

thud.etymology: Cf. AS. a whirlwind, violent wind, or E. thump.

thumb.etymology: OE. thombe, thoumbe, , AS. ; akin to OFries. th, D. duim, G. daumen, OHG. d, Icel. , Dan. tommelfinger, Sw. tunne, and perhaps to L. tumere to swell. *56. Cf. Thimble, Tumid.

thump.etymology: Probably of imitative origin; perhaps influenced by dump, v.t.

thunder.etymology: OE. , , , AS. ; akin to to stretch, to thunder, D. donder thunder, G. donner, OHG. donar, Icel. Thor, L. tonare to thunder, tonitrus thunder, Gr. tan to stretch. *52. See Thin, and cf. Astonish, Detonate, Intone, Thursday, Tone.

thursday.etymology: OE. , , from the Scand. name Thor + E. day. Icel. Thor, the god of thunder, is akin to AS. thunder; D. Donderdag Thursday, G. Donnerstag, Icel. , Sw. & Dan. Torsdag. *52. See Thor, Thunder, and Day.

thus.etymology: L. thus, better tus, frankincense. See Thurible.

thwack.etymology: Cf. OE. thakken to stroke, AS. , E. whack.

thwart.etymology: OE. , , a. and adv., Icel. , neut. of athwart, transverse, across; akin to AS. perverse, transverse, cross, D. dwars, OHG. dwerah, twerh, G. zwerch, quer, Dan. & Sw. tver athwart, transverse, Sw. tvär cross, unfriendly, Goth. angry. Cf. Queer.

thyme.etymology: OE. tyme, L. thymum, Gr. thym; -- perhaps so named because of its sweet smell. Cf. Fume, n.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that the substance in the name of which it appears belongs to the series of alcohols or hydroxyl derivatives, as carbinol, glycerol, etc.

tibial.etymology: L. tibialis, fr. tibia the shin bone; also, a pipe or flute, originally made of a bone: cf. F. tibial.

ticket.etymology: F. étiquette a label, ticket, fr. OF. estiquette, or OF. etiquet, estiquet; both of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. stick. See Stick, n. & v., and cf. Etiquette, Tick credit.

ticking.etymology: From Tick a bed cover. Cf. Ticken.

tickle.etymology: Perhaps freq. of tick to beat; pat; but cf. also AS. citelian to tickle, D. kittelen, G. kitzlen, OHG. chizzilon, chuzzilon, Icel. kitla. Cf. Kittle, v. t.

tickseed.etymology: Tick the insect + seed; cf. G. wanzensamen, literally, bug seed.

ticktack.etymology: See Tick to beat, to pat, and (for sense 2) cf. Tricktrack.

tide.etymology: AS. tid time; akin to OS. & OFries. tid, D. tijd, G. zeit, OHG. zit, Icel. ti, Sw. & Dan. tid, and probably to Skr. aditi unlimited, endless, where a- is a negative prefix. *58. Cf. Tidings, Tidy, Till, prep., Time.

tidings.etymology: OE. tidinge, ti, tidinde, from or influenced by Icel. ti; akin to Dan. tidende, Sw. tidning, G. zeung, AS. tidan to happen, E. betide, tide. See Tide, v. i. & n.

tidy.etymology: From Tide time, season; cf. D. tijdig timely, G. zeitig, Dan. & Sw. tidig.

tie.etymology: AS. tege, t, tige. *64. See Tie, v. t.

tierce.etymology: F. tierce a third, from tiers, tierce, third, fr. L. tertius the third; akin to tres three. See Third, Three, and cf. Terce, Tercet, Tertiary.

tiercel.etymology: OE. tercel, tercelet, F. tiercelet, a dim. of (assumed) tiercel, or LL. tertiolus, dim. fr. L. tertius the third; -- so called, according to some, because every third bird in the nest is a male, or, according to others, because the male is the third part less than female. Cf. Tercel.

tiff.etymology: Originally, a sniff, sniffing; cf. Icel. a smell, to sniff, Norw. tev a drawing in of the breath, teva to sniff, smell, dial. Sw. tüv smell, scent, taste.

tiffany.etymology: OE. tiffenay; cf. OF. tiffe ornament, tiffer to adjust, adorn. See Tiff to dress.

tiffin.etymology: Properly, tiffing a quaffing, a drinking. See Tiff, n.

tiger.etymology: OE. tigre, F. tigre, L. tigris, Gr. ti`gris; probably of Persian origin; cf. Zend tighra pointed, tighri an arrow, Per. tir; perhaps akin to E. stick, v.t.; -- probably so named from its quickness.

tight.etymology: OE. tight, thiht; probably of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. , Dan. tæt, Sw. tät: akin to D. & G. dicht thick, tight, and perhaps to E. thee to thrive, or to thick. Cf. Taut.

tike.etymology: Icel. tik a bitch; akin to Sw. tik.

tilde.etymology: Sp., fr. L. titulus a superscription, title, token, sign. See Title, n.

tiler.etymology: Of uncertain origin, but probably from E. tile, n.

tillandsia.etymology: NL. So named after Prof. Tillands, of Abo, in Finland.

tilt.etymology: OE. telt (perhaps from the Danish), teld, AS. teld, geteld; akin to OD. telde, G. zelt, Icel. tjald, Sw. tält, tjäll, Dan. telt, and ASThe beteldan to cover.

tilth.etymology: AS. til, fr. tilian to till. See Till to cultivate.

timbale.etymology: F., prop., a kettledrum; -- so named from the form of the mold used. Cf. Timbal.

timber.etymology: Probably the same word as timber sort of wood; cf. Sw. timber, LG. timmer, MHG. zimber, G. zimmer, F. timbre, LL. timbrium. Cf. Timmer.

timbre.etymology: F., a bell to be struck with a hammer, sound, tone, stamp, crest, in OF., a timbrel. Cf. Timbrel.

timbrel.etymology: Dim. of OE. timbre, OF. timbre; probably fr. L. typmanum, Gr. tabl a drum; cf. Per. tambal a drum. See Tympanum, and cf. 2d Timbre, Tymbal.

time.etymology: OE. time, AS. tima, akin to tid time, and to Icel. timi, Dan. time an hour, Sw. timme. *58. See Tide, n.

timid.etymology: L. timidus, fr. timere to fear; cf. Skr. tam to become breathless, to become stupefief: cf. F. timide.

timorous.etymology: LL. timorosus, from L. timor fear; akin to timere to fear. See Timid.

timothy.etymology: From Timothy Hanson, who carried the seed from New England to Maryland about 1720.

tin.etymology: As. tin; akin to D. tin, G. zinn, OHG. zin, Icel. & Dan. tin, Sw. tenn; of unknown origin.

tinamou.etymology: From the native name: cf. F. tinamous.

tinct.etymology: L. tinctus, p.p. of tingere to tinge. See Tinge.

tincture.etymology: L. tinctura a dyeing, from tingere, tinctum, to tinge, dye: cf. OE. tainture, teinture, F. teinture, L. tinctura. See Tinge.

tindal.etymology: From the native name: cf. Malayalam ta.

tinder.etymology: OE. tinder, tunder, AS. tynder, tyndre; akin to tendan to kindle, D. tonder tinder, G. zunder, OHG. zuntara, zuntra, Icel. tundr, Sw. tunder, Dan. tönder. See Tind.

tinge.etymology: L. tingere, tinctum, to dye, stain, wet; akin to Gr. tunken to dip, OHG. tunchon, dunchon, thunkon. Cf. Distain, Dunker, Stain, Taint a stain, to stain, Tincture, Tint.

tink.etymology: OE. tinken; of imitative origin. Cf. Ting a tinkling, Tinker.

tinker.etymology: From Tink, because the tinker's way of proclaiming his trade is to beat a kettle, or because in his work he makes a tinkling noise. Johnson.

tinkle.etymology: Freq. of tink. See Tink, Tingle.

tinsel.etymology: F. étincelle a spark, OF. estincelle, L. scintilla. Cf. Scintillate, Stencil.

tint.etymology: For older tinct, fr. L. tinctus, p.p. of tingere to dye: cf. F. teinte, teint, It. tinta, tinto. See Tinge, and cf. Taint to stain, a stain, Tent a kind of wine, Tinto.

tiny.etymology: Probably fr. tine, teen, trouble, distress, vexation.

tip.etymology: Akin to D. & Dan. tip, LG. & Sw. tipp, G. zipfel, and probably to E. tap a plug, a pipe.

tippet.etymology: OE. tipet, tepet, AS. tæppet, probably fr. L. tapete tapestry, hangings. Cf. Tape, Tapestry, Tapet.

tipple.etymology: From tip a small end, or a word akin to it; cf. Norw. tipla to tipple, to drip, Prov. E. tip, tiff, tift, a draught of liquor, dial. G. zipfeln to eat and drink in small parts. See Tip a point, and cf. Tipsy.

tipsy.etymology: Akin to tipple; cf. Prov. G. tips drunkenness, betipst drunk, tipsy. See Tipple.

tirade.etymology: F., fr. It. tirada, properly, a pulling; hence, a lengthening out, a long speech, a tirade, fr. tirare to draw; of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. tear to redn. See Tear to rend, and cf. Tire to tear.

tire.etymology: Aphetic form of attire; OE. tir, a tir. See Attire.

tissue.etymology: F. tissu, fr. tissu, p.p. of tisser, tistre, to weave, fr. L. texere. See Text.

tithe.etymology: OE. tithe, tethe, properly an adj., tenth, AS. teó the tenth; akin to tién, t, ten, ten, G. zehnte, adj., tenth, n., a tithe, Icel. tiund the tenth; tithe, Goth. taíhunda tenth. See Ten, and cf. Tenth, Teind.

title.etymology: OF. title, F. titre, L. titulus an inscription, label, title, sign, token. Cf. Tilde, Titrate, Titular.

titmouse.etymology: OE. titemose, titmase; tit small, or a small bird + AS. mase a kind of small bird; akin to D. mees a titmouse, G. meise, OHG. meisa, Icel. meisingr. The English form has been influenced by the unrelated word mouse. Cf. Tit a small bird.

titrate.etymology: F. titrer, from titre standard, title. See Title, n.

tittle.etymology: OE. titel, titil, apparently a dim. of tit, in the sense of small; cf. G. tüttel a tittle, dim. of OHG. tutta teat. Perhaps, however, the same word as title, n.

titular.etymology: F. titulaire, fr. L. titulus. See Title.

toad.etymology: OE. tode, tade, AS. tadie, tadige; of unknown origin. Cf. Tadpole.

toast.etymology: OF. toster to roast, toast, fr. L. torrere, tostum, to parch, roast. See Torrid.

tobacco.etymology: Sp. tabaco, fr. the Indian tabaco the tube or pipe in which the Indians or Caribbees smoked this plant. Some derive the word from Tabaco, a province of Yucatan, where it was said to be first found by the Spaniards; others from the island of Tobago, one of the Caribbees. But these derivations are very doubtful.

toboggan.etymology: Corruption of American Indian odabagan a sled.

toccata.etymology: It., fr. toccare to touch. See Touch.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

tocsin.etymology: F., fr. OF. toquier to touch, F. toquer (originally, a dialectic form of F. toucher) + seint (for sein) a bell, LL. signum, fr. L. signum a sign, signal. See Touch, and Sign.

tod.etymology: Akin to D. todde a rag, G. zotte shag, rag, a tuft of hair, Icel. toddi a piece of a thing, a tod of wool.

toddy.etymology: Formed from Hind. ta the juice of the palmyra tree, popularly, toddy, fr. ta the palmyra tree, Skr. tala.

tody.etymology: Cf. NL. todus, F. todier, G. todvogel.

toe.etymology: OE. too, taa, AS. ta; akin to D. teen, G. zehe, OHG. zeha, Icel. ta, Sw. tå, Dan. taa; of uncertain origin. *60.

toga.etymology: L., akin to tegere to cover. See Thatch.

together.etymology: OE. togedere, togidere, AS. togædere, togædre, togadere; to to + gador together. *29. See To, prep., and Gather.

toil.etymology: F. toiles, pl., toils, nets, fr. toile cloth, canvas, spider web, fr. L. tela any woven stuff, a web, fr. texere to weave. See Text, and cf. Toilet.

toilet.etymology: F. toilette, dim. of toile cloth. See Toil a net.

token.etymology: OE. token, taken, AS. tacen; akin to OFries. teken, OS. tekan, D. teeken, G. zeichen, OHG. Zeihhan, Icel. takan, teiken, Sw. tecken, Dan. tegn, Goth. taikns sign, token, gateihan to tell, show, AS. teón to accuse, G. zeihen, OHG. zihan, G. zeigen to show, OHG. zeigon, Icel. tja, L. dicere to say, Gr. di. Cf. Diction, Teach.

tole.etymology: OE. tollen to draw, to entice; of uncertain origin. Cf. Toll to ring a bell.

tolerable.etymology: L. tolerabilis: cf. F. tolérable. See Tolerate.

tolerant.etymology: L. tolerans, p.pr. of tolerare to tolerate: cf. F. tolérant. See Tolerate.

tolerate.etymology: L. toleratus, p.p. of tolerare, fr. the same root as tollere to lift up, tuli, used as perfect of ferre to bear, latus (for tlatus), used as p.p. of ferre to bear, and E. thole. See Thole, and cf. Atlas, Collation, Delay, Elate, Extol, Legislate, Oblate, Prelate, Relate, Superlative, Talent, Toll to take away, Translate.

tomahawk.etymology: Of American Indian origin; cf. Algonkin tomehagen, Mohegan tumnahegan, Delaware tamoihecan.

tomato.etymology: Sp. or Pg. tomate, of American Indian origin; cf. Mexican tomail.

tomb.etymology: OE. tombe, toumbe, F. tombe, LL. tumba, fr. Gr. tumulus a mound. Cf. Tumulus.

tombac.etymology: Pg. tambaca,tambaque, fr. Malay tambaga copper; cf. Skr. tamraka; cf. F. tombac.

tomboy.etymology: Tom (for Thomas, L. Thomas, fr. Gr. boy.

tome.etymology: F. tome (cf. It., Sp., & Pg. tomo), L. tomus, fr. Gr. tondere to shear, E. tonsure. Cf. Anatomy, Atom, Entomology, Epitome.

tomentose.etymology: L. tomentum a stuffing of wool, hair, or feathers: cf. F. tomenteux.

tone.etymology: F. ton, L. tonus a sound, tone, fr. Gr. Thin, and cf. Monotonous, Thunder, Ton fasion,Tune.

tongs.etymology: OE. tonge, tange, AS. tange; akin to D. tang, G. zanga, OHG. zanga, Don. tang, Sw. tng, Icel. tng, Gr. dadaTang a strong taste, anything projecting.

tongue.etymology: OE. tunge, tonge, AS. tunge; akin to OFries. tunge, D. tong, OS. tunga, G. zunge, OHG. zunga, Icel. & Sw. tunga, Dan tunge, Goth. tugdingua, L. lingua. Language, Lingo.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

tonsorial.etymology: L. tonsorius, fr. tonsor a shearer, barber, fr. tondere, tonsum, to shear. See Tonsure.

tonsure.etymology: F., fr. L. tonsura a shearing, clipping, from tondere, tonsum, to shear, shave; cf. Gr. tome.

tontine.etymology: F., from It. tontina; -- so called from its inventor, Tonti, an Italian, of the 17th century.

tonus.etymology: L. a sound, tone. See Tone.

too.etymology: The same word as to, prep. See To.

tool.etymology: OE. tol,tool. AS. tl; akin to Icel. tl, Goth. taijan to do, to make, taui deed, work, and perhaps to E. taw to dress leather. sq. root64.

toot.etymology: OE. toten, AS. totian to project; hence, to peep out.

tooth.etymology: OE. toth,tooth, AS. ttth, OS. & D. tand, OHG. zang, zan, G. zahn, Icel. tnn, Sw. & Dan. tand, Goth. tumpus, Lith. dantis, W. dant, L. dens, dentis, Gr. danta; probably originally the p. pr. of the verb to eat. *239. Cf. Eat, Dandelion, Dent the tooth of a wheel, Dental, Dentist, Indent, Tine of a fork, Tusk.

top.etymology: CF. OD. dop, top, OHG., MNG., & dial. G. topf; perhaps akin to G. topf a pot.

topaz.etymology: OE. topas, F. topaze, L. topazos, or topazion, a kind of precious stone, Gr. to`pazos, topa`zion; possibly akin to Skr. tap to glow (cf. Tepid). According to some, the name is from Topazos, a small island in the Red Sea, where the Romans obtained a stone which they called by this name, but which is the chrysolite of the moderns.

tope.etymology: Probably from Skr. stpa a tope, astupa, through Prakrin tppo.

tophus.etymology: NL.: cf. F. tophus a mineral concretion in the joint. See Toph.

topic.etymology: F. topiques, pl., L. topica the title of a work of Aristotle, Gr. topika`, fr. topiko`s of or for place, concerning to`poi, or commonplaces, fr. to`pos a place.

topical.etymology: Cf. F. topique, LL. topicus, Gr. Topic, n.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

toque.etymology: F. toque; of Celtic origin; cf. W.toc.

tor.etymology: AS. torr; cf. Gael. torr. Cf. Tower.

torch.etymology: OE. torche, F. torche a torch, rag, wisp, pad; probably from a derivative of L. torquere, tortum, to twist, because twisted like a rope; cf. F. torcher to rub, wipe, It. topcia a torch, torciare to wrap, twist, OF. torse a torse. Cf. Torture.

tore.etymology: Probably from the root of tear; cf. W. tór a break, cut, tóri to break, cut.

toreador.etymology: Sp.,fr. torear to fight bulls, fr.L. taurus a bull.

torment.etymology: OF. torment, F. tourment, fr. L. tormentum an engine for hurling missiles, an instrument of torture, a rack, torture, fr. torquere to turn, to twist, hurl. See Turture.

tornado.etymology: From Sp. or Pg. tornar to turn, return, L. tornare to turn, hence, a whirling wind. The Sp. & Pg. tornada is a return. See Turn.

torpedo.etymology: L. torpedo, -inis, from torpere to be stiff, numb, or torpid. See Torpid.

torpid.etymology: L. torpidus, fr. torpere to be stiff, numb, or torpid; of uncertain origin.

torpor.etymology: L., from torpere, to be torpid.

torque.etymology: L. torques a twisted neck chain, fr. torquere to twist.

torrent.etymology: F., fr. L. torrens, -entis, fr. torrens burning, roaring, boiling, p. pr. of torrere to dry by heat, to burn. See Torrid.

torrid.etymology: L. torridus, fr. torrere to parch, to burn, akin to E. Thist: cf. F. torride. See Thirst.

torsion.etymology: F., fr. LL. torsio, fr. L. torquere, tortum, to twist. See Torture.

torsk.etymology: Dan.; akin to Icel. þorskr a codfish, G. dorsch.

torso.etymology: It. torso, probably fr. L. thyrsus a stalk, stem, thyrsus, Gr. torso, turso, a stalk, stem, G. dorsche a cabbage stalk. Cf. Thyrsus, Truss.

tort.etymology: F., from LL. tortum, fr. L. tortus twisted, crooked, p. p. of torqure to twist, bend. See Torture.

torticollis.etymology: F. toricolis; L. torquere, tortum, to twist + collum the neck.

tortoise.etymology: OE. tortuce, fr. OF. tortis crooked, fr. L. tortus isted, crooked, contorted, p.p. of torquere, tortum, to wind; cf. F. tortue tortoise, LL. tortuca, tartuca, Pr. tortesa crookedness, tortis crooked. so called in allusion to its crooked feet. See Torture.

tortrix.etymology: NL., fr. L. torquere, tortum, to twist.

tortuous.etymology: OE. tortuos, L.tortuosus, fr.tortus a twisting, winding, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist: cf. F. tortueux. See Torture.

torture.etymology: F.,fr.L. tortura, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist, rack, torture; probably akin to Gr. tre`pein to turn, G. drechsein to turn on a lathe, and perhaps to E. queer. Cf. Contort, Distort, Extort, Retort, Tart, n., Torch, Torment, Tortion, Tort, Trope.

torulose.etymology: L. torulus, dim. of torus: cf. F. toruleux. See Torus

torus.etymology: L., a round, swelling, or bulging place, an elevation. Cf. 3d Tore.

tory.etymology: Properly used of the Irish bogtrotters who robbed and plundered during the English civil wars, professing to be in sympathy with the royal cause; hence transferred to those who sought to maintain the extreme prerogatives of the crown; probably from Ir. toiridhe, tor, a pursuer; akin to Ir. & Gael. toir a pursuit.

tosh.etymology: Cf. OF. tonce shorn, clipped, and E. tonsure.

total.etymology: F., fr. LL. totalis, fr. L. tolus all,whole. Cf. Factotum, Surtout, Teetotum.

tote.etymology: Said to be of African origin.

totem.etymology: Massachusetts Indian wutohtimoin that to which a person or place belongs.

totter.etymology: Probably for older tolter; cf. AS. tealtrian to totter, vacillate. Cf.Tilt to incline, Toddle, Tottle, Totty.

toucan.etymology: F., fr. Pg. tucano; from Brazilian name.

touch.etymology: F. toucher, OF. touchier, tuchier; of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. zucchen, zukken, to twitch, pluck, draw, G. zukken, zukken, v. intens. fr. OHG. ziohan to draw, G. ziehen, akin to E. tug. See Tuck, v. t., Tug, and cf. Tocsin, Toccata.

touchwood.etymology: Probably for tachwood; OE. tache tinder (of uncertain origin) + wood.

tough.etymology: OE. tough, AS. toh, akin to D. taai, LG. taa, tage, tau, OHG. zahi, G. zähe, and also to AS. getenge near to, close to, oppressive, OS. bitengi.

toupee.etymology: F. toupet, dim. of OF. top a tuft; of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. top. See Top apex, and cf. Topet.

tourmaline.etymology: F. tourmaline, cf. It. turmalina, tormalina, NL. turmalina, turmalinus; all fr. tournamal, a name given to this stone in Ceylon.

tournament.etymology: OE. turnement, tornement, OF. torneiement, tornoiement, F. tournoiement a turning or wheeling round. See Tourney.

tourney.etymology: OF. tornei, tornoi, F. tournoi, fr. OF. torneier, tornoier, tournoier, to tit, to tourney, F. tournoyer to turn round and round. See Turn, v. t.

tow.etymology: OE. tow, AS. tow, akin to OD. touw, Icel. taw, v.t.

towel.etymology: OE.towaille, towail, F. touaille, LL. toacula, of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. dwahila, swahilla, G. zwehle, fr. OHG. dwahan to wash; akin to D. dwaal a towel, AS. þweán to wash, OS. thwahan, Icel. þva, Sw. två, Dan. toe, Goth. þwahan. Cf. Doily.

tower.etymology: OE. tour,tor,tur, F. tour, L. turris; akin to Gr. twr a tower, Ir. tor a castle, Gael. torr a tower, castle. Cf. Tor, Turret.

towline.etymology: AS. tohline. See Tow, v. t., and Line.

town.etymology: OE. toun, tun, AS. tun inclosure, fence, village, town; akin to D. tuin a garden, G. zaun a hadge, fence, OHG. zun, Icel. tun an inclosure, homestead, house, Ir. & Gael. dun a fortress, W. din. Cf. Down, adv. & prep., Dune, tine to inclose.

toxic.etymology: L. toxicum poison, originally, a poison in which arrows were dipped, Gr. Intoxicate.

toy.etymology: D. tuid tools, implements, stuff, trash, speeltuig playthings, toys; akin to G. zeug stuff, materials, MNG. zuic, Icel. tygi gear; all ultimately from the root of E. tug, v.t.; cf.G. zeugen to beget, MHG.ziugen to beget, make ready, procure. See Tug, v. t.

trace.etymology: F.trais. pl. of trait. See Trait.

trachea.etymology: NL.,from L. trachia, Gr. trachei^a (sc. trachée.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

track.etymology: OF.trac track of horses, mules, trace of animals; of Teutonic origin; cf.D.trek a drawing, trekken to draw, travel, march, MHG. trechen, pret. trach. Cf. Trick.

tractable.etymology: L. tractabilis, fr, tractare to draw violently, to handle, treat. See Treat, v. t.

traction.etymology: L. trahere, tractum, to draw: cf. F. traction.

tractor.etymology: NL., from L. trahere, tractum, to draw.

trade.etymology: Formerly, a path, OE. tred a footmark. See Tread, n. & v.

tradition.etymology: OE. tradicioun, L. traditio, from tradere to give up, transmit. See Treason, Traitor.

traduce.etymology: L. traducere, traductum, to lead across, lead along, exhibit as a spectacle, disgrace, transfer, derive; trans across, over + ducere to lead: cf. F. traduire to transfer, translate, arraign, fr. L. traducere. See Duke.

traffic.etymology: F. trafiquer; cf. It. trafficare, Sp. traficar, trafagar, Pg. traficar, trafegar, trafeguear, LL. traficare; of uncertain origin, perhaps fr. L. trans across, over + -ficare to make (see -fy, and cf. G. übermachen to transmit, send over, e. g., money, wares); or cf. Pg. trasfegar to pour out from one vessel into another, OPg. also, to traffic, perhaps fr. (assumed) LL. vicare to exchange, from L. vicis change (cf. Vicar).

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

tragacanth.etymology: L. tragacanthum tragacanth, tragacantha the plant producing tragacanth, Gr. tragacanthe.

tragedy.etymology: OE.tragedie, OF.tragedie, F. tragédie, L. tragoedia, Gr. trout) + Ode.

trail.etymology: OE. trailen, OF. trailler to trail a deer, or hunt him upon a cold scent, also, to hunt or pursue him with a limehound, F. trailler to trail a fishing line; probably from a derivative of L. trahere to draw; cf. L. traha a drag, sledge, tragula a kind of drag net, a small sledge, Sp. trailla a leash, an instrument for leveling the ground, D. treilen to draw with a rope, to tow, treil a rope for drawing a boat. See Trace, v. t.

train.etymology: OF. trahiner, traïner,F. traîner, LL. trahinare, trainare, fr. L. trahere to draw. See Trail.

traipse.etymology: Cf. G. trapsen, trappsen, trappen, to tread noisily, to walk stamping. See Trample, Trape.

trait.etymology: F., fr. L. tractus, fr. trahere to draw. See Trace, v., and cf. Tract a region, Trace a strap, Tret.

traitor.etymology: OE. traitour, OF. traïtor, traïteur, F. treître, L. traditor, fr. tradere, traditum, to deliver, to give up or surrender treacherously, to betray; trans across, over + dare to give. See Date time, and cf. Betray,Tradition, Traditor, Treason.

tralatitious.etymology: L. tralatitius, translatitius, tralaticius, translaticius. See Tralation.

tram.etymology: Prov. E. tram a coal wagon, the shaft of a cart or carriage, a beam or bar; probably of Scand, origin; cf. OSw. tråm, trum, a beam, OD. drom, Prov. & OHG. tram.

trammel.etymology: F. tramail, trémail, a net, LL. tremaculum, tremacle, a kind of net for taking fish; L. tres three + macula a mesh. See Three, and Mail armor.

tramontane.etymology: OF. tramontain, It. tramontano, L. transmontanus; trans across, beyond + mons, montis, mountain.

tramp.etymology: OE. trampen; akin to LG. trampen, G. trampeln, LG. & D. trappen, Dan. trampe, Sw. & Icel. trampa, Goth. anatrimpan to press upon; also to D. trap a step, G. treppe steps, stairs. Cf. Trap a kind of rock, Trape, Trip, v. i., Tread.

tranquil.etymology: L. tranquillus; probably fr. trans across, over + a word akin to quietus quiet: cf. F. tranquille. See Quiet.

transact.etymology: L. transactus, p. p. of transigere. See Transaction.

transaction.etymology: L. transactio, fr. transigere, transactum, to drive through, carry through, accomplish, transact; trans across, over + agere to drive; cf. F. transaction. See Act, Agent.

transalpine.etymology: L. transalpinus; trans across, beyond + Alpinus Alpine, from Alpes the Alps: cf. F. transalpin.

transatlantic.etymology: Pref. trans- + Atlantic: cf. F. transatlantique.

transcendent.etymology: L. transcendens, -entis, p. pr. of transcendere to transcend: cf. F. transcendant, G. transcendent.

transduction.etymology: L. transducere, traducere, -dictum, to lead across or over. See Traduce.

transept.etymology: Pref. trans- + L. septum an inclosure. See Septum.

transfix.etymology: L. transfixus, p. p. of transfigure to transfix; trans across, through + figere to fix, fasten. See Fix.

transform.etymology: L. transformare, transformatum; trans across, over + formare to from: cf. F. transformer. See Form, v. t.

transfuse.etymology: L. transfusus, p. p. of transfundere: cf. F. transfuser. See Transfund.

transient.etymology: L. transiens, -entis, p. pr. of transire, transitum, to go or pass over. See Trance.

transit.etymology: L. transitus, from transire to go over: cf. F. transit. See Transient.

transplant.etymology: F. transplanter, L. transplantare; trans across, over + plantare to plant. See Plant.

transport.etymology: F. transporter, L. transportare; trans across + portare to carry. See Port bearing, demeanor.

transpose.etymology: F. transposer; pref. trans- (L. trans across) + poser to put. See Pose.

transude.etymology: Pref. trans- + L. sudare to sweat: cf. F. transsuder.

trappings.etymology: From Trap to dress with ornaments.

trash.etymology: Cf. Icel. tros rubbish, leaves, and twigs picked up for fuel, trassi a slovenly fellow, Sw. trasa a rag, tatter.

travail.etymology: F. travail; cf. Pr. trabalh, trebalh, toil, torment, torture; probably from LL. trepalium a place where criminals are tortured, instrument of torture. But the French word may be akin to L. trabs a beam, or have been influenced by a derivative from trabs (cf. Trave). Cf. Travel.

trave.etymology: Through French, fr. L. trabs, trabis, a beam; cf. OF. tref a beam, also F. travail a frame to confine a horse, OE. trave, trevys, travise, It. travaglio, F. travée the space between two beams.

travel.etymology: Properly, to labor, and the same word as travail.

traverse.etymology: OF. travers, L. transversus, p. p. of transvertere to turn or direct across. See Transverse, and cf. Travers.

travesty.etymology: F. travesti, p. p. of travestir to disguise, to travesty, It. travestire, fr. L. trans across, over + vestire to dress, clothe. See Vest.

trawl.etymology: OF. trauler, troller, F. trôter, to drag about, to stroll about; probably of Teutonic origin. Cf. Troll, v. t.

tray.etymology: OF. traïr, F. trahir, L. tradere. See Traitor.

treachery.etymology: OE. trecherïe, trichere, OF. trecherie, tricherie, F. tricherie trickery, from tricher to cheat, to trick, OF. trichier, trechier; probably of Teutonic origin. See Trickery, Trick.

treacle.etymology: OE. triacle a sovereign remedy, theriac, OF. triacle, F. thériaque (cf. Pr. triacla, tiriaca, Sp. & It. triaca, teriaca), L. theriaca an antidote against the bite of poisonous animals, Gr. qhri`on a beast, a wild beast, dim. of qh`r a beast. Cf. Theriac.

tread.etymology: OE. treden, AS. tredan; akin to OFries. treda, OS. tredan, D. & LG. treden, G. treten, OHG. tretan, Icel. tro, Sw. tråda, träda, Dan. træde, Goth. trudan, and perhaps ultimately to F. tramp; cf. Gr. dram to run. Cf. Trade, Tramp, Trot.

treadle.etymology: OE. tredyl a step, AS. tredel. See Tread.

treason.etymology: OE. tresun, treisun, traisoun, OF. traïson, F. trahison, L. traditio a giving up, a delivering up, fr. tradere to give up, betray. See Traitor, and cf. Tradition.

treasure.etymology: OE. tresor, tresour, F. trésor, L. thesaurus, Gr. Thesis, and cf. Thesaurus.

treat.etymology: OE. treten, OF. traitier, F. traiter, from L. tractare to draw violently, to handle, manage, treat, v. intens. from trahere, tractum, to draw. See Trace, v. t., and cf. Entreat, Retreat, Trait.

treatise.etymology: OE. tretis, OF. treitis, traitis, well made. See Treat.

treaty.etymology: OE. tretee, F. traité, LL. tractatus; cf. L. tractatus a handling, treatment, consultation, tractate. See Treat, and cf. Tractate.

trebuchet.etymology: OF. trebuchet, trebukiet, an engine of war for hurling stones, F. trébuchet a gin, trap, a kind of balance, fr. OF. trebuchier, trebuquier, to stumble, trip, F. trébucher.

trebucket.etymology: OF. trebuchet, trebukiet, an engine of war for hurling stones, F. trébuchet a gin, trap, a kind of balance, fr. OF. trebuchier, trebuquier, to stumble, trip, F. trébucher.

tree.etymology: OE. tree, tre, treo, AS. treó, treów, tree, wood; akin to OFries. tr, OS. treo, trio, Icel. tr, Dan. træ, Sw. trä, träd, Goth. triu, Russ. drevo, W. derw an oak, Ir. darag, darog, Gr. dru tree, wood, daru wood. Dryad, Germander, Tar, n., Trough.

tremella.etymology: NL., fr. L. tremere, to tremble: cf. It. tremella, F. tremelle.

tremendous.etymology: L. tremendus that is to be trembled at, fearful, fr. tremere to tremble. See Tremble.

tremolite.etymology: From Tremola, a valley in the Alps, where it was discovered.

tremor.etymology: L., from tremere to tremble. See Tremble, v.

trenchant.etymology: OF. trenchant, F. tranchant, p. pr. See Trench, v. t.

trencher.etymology: OE. trencheoir, F. tranchoir, fr. trancher to cut, carve. See Trench, v. t.

trend.etymology: OE. trenden to roll or turn about; akin to OFries. trind, trund, round, Dan. & Sw. trind, AS. trendel a circle, ring, and E. trendle, trundle.

trental.etymology: LL. trentale, fr. L. triginta thirty; akin to tres three: cf. OF. trentel. See Three, and cf. Trigintal.

trepan.etymology: F. trépan (cf. Sp. trépano, It. trepano, trapano), LL. trepanum, fr. Gr. Trephine.

trephine.etymology: A dim. of 1st trepan: cf. F. tréphine.

trepidation.etymology: F. trépidation, L. trepidatio, fr. trepidare to hurry with alarm, to tremble, from trepidus agitated, disturbed, alarmed; cf. trepit he turns, Gr. torture.

trespass.etymology: OF. trespasser to go across or over, transgress, F. trépasser to die; pref. tres- (L. trans across, over) + passer to pass. See Pass, v. i., and cf. Transpass.

tress.etymology: OE. tresse, OF. trece, F. tresse, LL. tricia, fr. Gr. tri`cha threefold, because a tress is usually formed by interlacing three pieces; akin to trei^s three. See Three.

triumph.etymology: L. triumphus, OL. triumpus; of uncertain origin; cf. Gr. triomphe. Cf. Trump at cards.

triumphant.etymology: L. triumphans, p. pr. of triumphare: cf. F. triomphant. See Triumph, v. i.

triumvir.etymology: L., fr. res, gen. trium, three + vir a man. See Three, and Virile.

triune.etymology: Pref. tri- + L. unus one. See One.

trivet.etymology: Probably through French fr. L. tripes, -edis, three-footed; tri- (see Tri-)+ pes, pedis, foot: cf. F. trépied. See Foot, and cf. Tripod.

trivial.etymology: L. trivialis, properly, that is in, or belongs to, the crossroads or public streets; hence, that may be found everywhere, common, fr. trivium a place where three roads meet, a crossroad, the public street; tri- (see Tri-) + via a way: cf. F. trivial. See Voyage.
