troat.etymology: Either onomatopoetic, or akin to throat.

troche.etymology: Gr. trocho`s anything round or circular, a wheel, properly, a runner, fr. tre`chein to run. Cf. Trochee.

trochee.etymology: L. trochaeus, Gr. Troche, Truck a wheel.

trojan.etymology: L. Trojanus, fr. Troja, Troia, Troy, from Tros, Gr. Trw`s, Trwo`s, Tros, the mythical founder of Troy.

trollop.etymology: From Troll to roll, to stroll; but cf. also Trull.

trombone.etymology: It., aug. of tromba a trumpet: cf. F. trombone. See Trump a trumpet.

troop.etymology: F. troupe, OF. trope, trupe, LL. troppus; of uncertain origin; cf. Icel. þorp a hamlet, village, G. dorf a village, dial. G. dorf a meeting. Norw. torp a little farm, a crowd, E. thorp. Cf. Troupe.

trope.etymology: L. tropus, Gr. Torture, and cf. Trophy, Tropic, Troubadour, Trover.

trophy.etymology: F. trophée (cf. It. & Sp. trofeo), L. tropaeum, trophaeum, Gr. Trope.

roots.meaning: A suffix, denoting that the element indicated enters into certain compounds with its highest valence, or with a valence relatively higher than in compounds where the name of the element ends in -ous; as, ferric, sulphuric. It is also used in the general sense of pertaining to; as, hydric, sodic, calcic.

tropical.etymology: Cf. L. tropicus of turning, Gr. Tropic, n.

roots.meaning: A suffix indicating an act, a process, the result of an act or a process, a state; also, a characteristic (as a theory, doctrine, idiom, etc.); as, baptism, galvanism, organism, hypnotism, socialism, sensualism, Anglicism.

trot.etymology: OE. trotten, OF. troter, F. trotter; probably of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. tread; cf. OHG. trott to tread. See Tread.

troth.etymology: A variant of truth. See Truth.

troubadour.etymology: F. troubadour, fr. Pr. trobador, (assumed) LL. tropator a singer, tropare to sing, fr. tropus a kind of singing, a melody, song, L. tropus a trope, a song, Gr. Trope, and cf. Trouv.

trouble.etymology: F. troubler, OF. trobler, trubler, tourbler,fr. (assumed) LL. turbulare, L. turbare to disorderly group, a little crowd; both from turba a disorder, tumult, crowd; akin to Gr. thorp; cf. Skr. tvar, tur,o hasten. Cf. Turbid.

trough.etymology: OE. trough, trogh, AS. trog, troh; akin to D., G., & Icel. trog, Sw. tråg, Dan. trug; probably originally meaning, made of wood, and akin to E. tree. Tree, and cf. Trug.

trounce.etymology: F. tronce, tronche, a stump, piece of wood. See Truncheon.

trousseau.etymology: F., fr. OF. trossel, dim. of trousse a bundle, truss. See Truss.

trowel.etymology: OE. truel, OF. truele, F. truelle, LL. truella, L. trulla, dim. of trua a ladle; probably akin to Gr. quirl a stirrer, MHG. twirel, OHG. dwiril, Icel. þvara, AS. þwiril. Cf. Twirl.

truant.etymology: F. truand, OF. truant, a vagrant, beggar; of Celtic origin; cf. W. tru, truan, wretched, miserable, truan a wretch, Ir. trogha miserable, Gael. truaghan a poor, distressed, or wretched creature, truagh wretched.

truce.etymology: OE. trewes, triwes, treowes, pl. of trewe a truce, properly, pledge of fidelity, truth, AS. treów fidelity, faith, troth. See True.

truck.etymology: L. trochus an iron hoop, Gr. Trochee, and cf. Truckle, v. i.

truckle.etymology: Dim. of truck a wheel; or from the kindred L. trochlea a block, sheaf containing one or more pulleys. See Truck a wheel.

truculent.etymology: L.truculentus, fr. trux, gen. trucis, wild, fierce: cf. F. truculent.

trudge.etymology: Perhaps of Scand. origin, and originally meaning, to walk on snowshoes; cf. dial. Sw. truga, trudja, a snowshoe, Norw. truga, Icel. þruga.

true.etymology: OE. trewe, AS. treówe faithful, true, from treów fidelity, faith, troth; akin to OFries. triuwe, adj., treuwa, n., OS. triuwi, adj., trewa, n., D.trouw, adj. & n., G. treu, adj., treue, n., OHG. gitriuwi, adj., triuwa, n., Icel. tryggr, adj., Dan. tro, adj. & n., Sw. trogen, adj., tro, n., Goth. triggws, adj., triggwa, n., trauan to trust, OPruss druwis faith. Cf. Trow, Trust, Truth.

truffle.etymology: OF. trufle, F. truffe; akin to Sp. trufa, tartufo; of uncertain origin; perhaps from L. tuber a tumor, knob, truffle. Cf. Tuber, Trifle.

trump.etymology: OE. trumpe, trompe, F. trompe; probably fr. L. triumphare to triumph, to exult, hence, probably, to make a joyous sound or noise. See Triumph, v. i. & n., and cf. Trombone, Tromp, Trump at cards, Trumpery, Trumpet, Trunk a proboscis.

trumpery.etymology: F. tromperie deceit, fr. tromper to deceive. See Trump to trick.

trumpet.etymology: F. trompette, dim. of trompe. See Trump a trumpet.

truncate.etymology: L. truncatus, p. p. of truncare to cut off, mutilate, fr. truncus maimed, mutilated, cut short. See Trunk.

truncheon.etymology: OE. tronchoun the shaft of a broken spear, broken piece, OF.tronchon, tron, F. tron, fr. OF. & F. tronce, tronche, a piece of wood; cf. OF. trons, tros, trois; all perhaps from L. thyrsus a stalk, stem, staff. See Thyrsus, and cf. Trounce.

trundle.etymology: AS. tryndel a little shield. See Trend, v. i.

trunk.etymology: F. tronc, L. truncus, fr. truncus maimed, mutilated; perhaps akin to torquere to twist wrench, and E. torture. Trunk in the sense of proboscis is fr. F. trompe (the same word as trompe a trumpet), but has been confused in English with trunk the stem of a tree (see Trump a trumpet). Cf. Truncate.

truss.etymology: OE. trusse, F. trousse, OF. also tourse; perhaps fr. L. tryrsus stalk, stem. Cf. Thyrsus, Torso, Trousers, Trousseau.

trust.etymology: OE. trust, trost, Icel. traust confidence, security; akin to Dan. & Sw. tröst comfort, consolation, G. trost, Goth. trausti a convention, covenant, and E. true. See True, and cf. Tryst.

truth.etymology: OE. treuthe, trouthe, treowpe, AS. treów. See True; cf. Troth, Betroth.

try.etymology: OE. trien to select, pick out, F. trier to cull, to out, LL. tritare to triturate (hence the sense of, to thresh, to separate the grain from the straw, to select), L. terere, tritum, to rub, bruise, grind, thresh. See Trite.

tryst.etymology: OE. trist, tryst, a variant of trust; cf. Icel. treysta to make trusty, fr. traust confidence, security. See Trust, n.

tub.etymology: OE. tubbe; of Dutch or Low German origin; cf. LG. tubbe, D. tobbe.

tube.etymology: L.tubus; akin to tuba a trumpet: cf F. tube.

tuber.etymology: L., a hump. knob; probably akin to tumere to swell. Cf. Tumid.

tubercle.etymology: L. tuberculum, dim. of tuber: cf. F. tubercule, OF. also tubercle. See Tuber.

tuberose.etymology: Cf. G. tuberose, F. tubéreuse, NL. Polianthes tuberosa. See Tuberous.

tuberous.etymology: L. tuberosus: cf. F. tubéreux. See Tuber, and cf. also Tuberose.

tubular.etymology: L. tubulus, dim. of tubus a tube, or pipe. See Tube.

tubule.etymology: F. tubule, or L. tubulus, dim. of tubus a tube, a pipe.

tuck.etymology: F. estoc; cf. It. stocco; both of German origin, and akin to E. stock. See Stock.

tucket.etymology: It toccata a prelude, fr. toccare to touch. See Toccata, Touch.

tuesday.etymology: OE. Tewesday, AS. Tiwes dæg the day of Tiw the god of war; akin to OHG. Zio, Icel. T, L. Jupiter, Gr. Ziostac Tuesday, G. Dienstag, Icel. T. See Deity, Day, and cf. Jovial.

tufa.etymology: It. fufo soft, sandy stone, L. tofus, tophus. Cf. Tofus, Toph, and Tophin.

tuft.etymology: Prov. E. tuff, F. touffe; of German origin; cf. G. zopf a weft of hair, pigtail, top of a tree. See Top summit.

tug.etymology: OE. toggen; akin to OD. tocken to entice, G. zucken to jerk, draw, Icel. toga to draw, AS. téon, p. p. togen, to draw, G. ziehen, OHG. ziohan, Goth. tiuhan, L. ducere to lead, draw. Cf. Duke, Team, Tie, v. t., Touch, Tow, v. t., Tuck to press in, Toy a plaything.

tuition.etymology: L. tuitio protection, guarding, from tueri, p. p. tuitus, to see, watch, protect: cf. F. tuition. Cf. Tutor.

tulip.etymology: F. tulipe, OF. also tulipan, It. tulipano, tulipa, from Turk. tulbend, dulbend, literally, a turban, Per. dulband; -- so called from the resemblance of the form of this flower to a turban. See Turban.

tulle.etymology: F.; -- so called from the town of Tulle, in France.

tumble.etymology: OE. tumblen, AS. tumbian to turn heels over head, to dance violently; akin to D. tuimelen to fall, Sw. tumla, Dan. tumle, Icel. tumba; and cf. G. taumeln to reel, to stagger.

tumbrel.etymology: OF. tomberel, F. tombereau, fr. tomber to fall, to tumble; of Teutonic origin. Cf. Tumble.

tumbril.etymology: OF. tomberel, F. tombereau, fr. tomber to fall, to tumble; of Teutonic origin. Cf. Tumble.

tumefy.etymology: F. tuméfier, fr. L. tumere to swell + -ficare (in comp.) to make; cf. L. tumefacere to tumefy. See Tumid, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

tumescence.etymology: L. tumescens, -entis, p.pr. of tumescere to swell up, v. incho. fr. tumere to swell.

tumid.etymology: L. tumidus, fr. tumere to swell; cf. Skr. tumra strong, fat. Cf. Thumb.

tumor.etymology: L., fr. tumere to swell: cf. F. tumeúr. See Tumid.

tumult.etymology: L.tumultus; probably akin to Skr. tumula noise, noisy, and perhaps to L. tumere to swell, E. tumid: cf. F. tumulte.

tumulus.etymology: L., a mound, a sepulchral mound, probably from tumere to swell. Cf. Tumid.

tun.etymology: AS. tunne. See Ton a weight.

tungsten.etymology: Sw. tungsten (cf. Dan. tungsteen, G. tungstein); tung heavy (akin to Dan. tung, Icel. þungr) + sten stone. See Stone.

tunicate.etymology: L. tunicatus, p. p. of tunicare to clothe with a tunic, fr. tunica a tunic.

tunnel.etymology: F. tonnelle a semicircular, wagon-headed vault, a tunnel net, an arbor, OF. also tonnel; dim. of tonne a tun; -- so named from its resemblance to a tun in shape. See Ton.

tunny.etymology: L. thunnus, thynnus, Gr. tonno, F. & Pr. thon.

tup.etymology: Probably akin to top summit, head.

tupelo.etymology: Tupelo, or tupebo, the native American Indian name.

turban.etymology: OE. turband, turbant, tolibant, F. turban, It. turbante, Turk. tulbend, dulbend, fr. Per. dulband. Cf. Tulip.

turbellaria.etymology: NL., dim. fr. L. turbo a whirling.

turbid.etymology: L. turbidus, from turba tumult, disturbance, akin to turbare to disturb. See Trouble, and cf. Disturb, Perturb.

turbinal.etymology: L. turbo, turben, -inis, a top, whirl.

turbinate.etymology: L. turbinatus, turbo, turben, - inis, a whirl, top.

turbine.etymology: L. turbo, -inis, that which spins or whirls round, whirl.

turbot.etymology: F.; -- probably so named from its shape, and from L. turbo a top, a whirl.

turbulent.etymology: L. turbulentus, fr. turba disorder, tumult: cf. F. turbulent. See Turbid.

tureen.etymology: F. terrine, L. terra earth. See Terrace.

turf.etymology: AS. turf; akin to D. turf peat, G. torf, OHG. zurba turf, Sw. & Icel. torf turf, peat, Dan. törv, Skr. darbha a kind of grass, a tuft of grass. sq. root242.

turgid.etymology: L. turgidus, from turgere to swell.

turk.etymology: Per. Turk; probably of Tartar origin: cf. F. Turc.

turmeric.etymology: F. terre-mérite, NL. terramerita, turmerica; apparently meaning, excellent earth, but perhaps a corruption of Ar. kurkum. Cf. Curcuma.

turmoil.etymology: Of uncertain origin; perhaps fr. OF. tremouille the hopper of a mill, trembler to tremble (cf. E. tremble); influenced by E. turn and moil.

turn.etymology: OE. turnen, tournen, OF. tourner, torner, turner, F. tourner, LL. tornare, fr. L. tornare to turn in a lathe, to rounds off, fr. tornus a lathe, Gr. throw. See Throw, and cf. Attorney, Return, Tornado, Tour, Tournament.

turnip.etymology: OE. turnep; probably fr. turn, or F. tour a turn, turning lathe + OE. nepe a turnip, AS. næpe, L. napus. Cf. Turn,v. t., Navew.

turnix.etymology: NL., fr. L. coturnix a quail.

turnverein.etymology: G., from turnen to exercise + verein a union.

turpentine.etymology: F. térébentine, OF. also turbentine; cf. Pr. terebentina, terbentina, It. terebentina, trementina; fr. L. terebinthinus of the turpentine tree, from terebinthus the turpentine tree. Gr. Terebinth.

turpitude.etymology: L. turpitudo, from turpis foul, base.

turquoise.etymology: F. turquoise; cf. Pr. & Sp. turquesa, It. turchese, turchina, LL. turchesius, turchina; -- so called because first brought from Turkey. See 1st Turkey.

turret.etymology: OE. touret, OF. tourette, dim. of tour a tower, L. turris. See Tower.

turtle.etymology: AS. turtle, L. turtur; probably of imitative origin. Cf. Turtle the sea tortoise.

tush.etymology: OE. tusch, AS. tusc; akin to OFries. tusk, tusch, and probably to AS. toedh tooth. See Tooth, and cf. Tusk.

tusk.etymology: OE. tusk, the same word as tusch, AS. tusc. See Tush a tooth.

tut.etymology: Cf. Sw. tut a point, pipe, tube, Dan. tut a cornet.

tutelage.etymology: L. tutela protection, fr. tutus safe, fr. tueri to watch, defend. Cf. Tuition.

tutelar.etymology: L. tutelaris: cf. F. tutélaire. See Tutelage.

tutelary.etymology: L. tutelaris: cf. F. tutélaire. See Tutelage.

tutor.etymology: OE. tutour, L. tutor, fr. tueri to watch, defend: cf. F. tuteur. Cf. Tuition.

tutsan.etymology: F. toutesaine; tout, toule, all (L. totus) + sain, saine, sound, healthy, L. sanus.

twain.etymology: OE. twein, tweien, tweyne, AS. twegen, masc. See Two.

twang.etymology: Of imitative origin; cf. Tang a sharp sound, Tinkle.

tweak.etymology: OE. twikken, originally the same word as twicchen; cf. LG. twikken. See Twitch.

tweed.etymology: Probably a corruption of twills. See Twill.

tweeze.etymology: OE. tweeze, tweese, fr. F. étuis, pl. of étui a case, sheath, box; probably of Teutonic origin; cf. MNG. stuche a wide sleeve in which articles could be carried, OHG. stuhha, G. stauche a short and narrow muff. Cf Etui, Tweezers.

twelfth.etymology: For twelft, OE. twelfte, AS. twelfta. See Twelve.

twelve.etymology: OE. twelve, twelf, AS. twelf; akin to OFries. twelf, twelef, twilif, OS. twelif, D. twaalf, G. zwölf, OHG. zwelif, Icel. t, Sw. tolf, Dan. tolv, Goth. twalif, from the root of E. two + the same element as in the second part of E. eleven. See Two, and Eleven.

twentieth.etymology: From Twenty; cf. AS. twentigo. See Twenty.

twenty.etymology: OE. twenty, AS. tw, twentig; akin to OFris. twintich, OS. tw, D. & LG. twintig, OHG. zweinzug, G. zwanzig, Goth. twai tigjis; that is, two tens. See Twain, Two, and Ten.

twice.etymology: OE. twies (where the s is the adverbial ending; see -wards), twie, AS. twiges, twiwa; akin to twi- (in comp.) two, G. zwie-, OHG. zwi-, Icel. tvi-, L. bi-, Gr. dvi-, and E. two. See Two.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

In the composition of chemical names bi- denotes two atoms, parts, or equivalents of that constituent to the name of which it is prefixed, to one of the other component, or that such constituent is present in double the ordinary proportion; as, bichromate, bisulphide. Be- and di- are often used interchangeably.

twiddle.etymology: Probably of imitative origin. Cf. Tweedle.

twilight.etymology: OE. twilight, AS. twi- (see Twice) + leóht light; hence the sense of doubtful or half light; cf. LG. twelecht, G. zwielicht. See Light.

twill.etymology: Scotch tweel; probably from LG. twillen to make double, from twi- two; akin to AS. twi-, E. twi- in twilight. See Twice, and cf. Tweed, Tweel.

twin.etymology: OE. twin double, AS. getwinne two and two, pl., twins; akin to D. tweeling a twin, G. zwilling, OHG. zwiniling, Icel. tvennr, tvinnr, two and two, twin, and to AS. twi- two. See Twice, Two.

twine.etymology: AS. twin, properly, a twisted or double thread; akin to D. twijn, Icel. twinni; from twi-. See Twice, and cf. Twin.

twinge.etymology: OE. twengen, AS. twengan; akin to OE. twingen to pain, afflict, OFries. thwinga, twinga, dwinga, to constrain, D. dwingen, OS. thwingan, G. zwingen, OHG. dwingan, thwingan, to press, oppress, overcome, Icel. þvinga, Sw. tvinga to subdue, constrain, Dan. twinge, and AS. þün to press, OHG. duhen, and probably to E. thong. Perhaps influenced by twitch. Cf. Thong.

twinkle.etymology: OE. twinklen, AS. twinclian; akin to OE. twinken to blink, wink, G. zwinken, zwinkern, and perhaps to E. twitch.

twirl.etymology: Cf. AS. þwiril a churn staff, a stirrer, flail, þweran, aþweran, to agitate, twirl, G. zwirlen, quirlen, to twirl, to turn round or about, quirl a twirling stick, OHG. dweran to twirl, stir. Cf. Trowel.

twist.etymology: OE. twisten, AS. twist a rope, as made of two (twisted) strands, fr. twi- two; akin to D. twist a quarrel, dissension, G. zwist, Dan. & Sw. tvist, Icel. twistr the deuce in cards, tvistr distressed. See Twice, Two.

twit.etymology: OE. atwiten, AS. ætwitan to reproach, blame; æt at + witan to reproach, blame; originally, to observe, see, hence, to observe what is wrong (cf. the meanings of E. animadvert; akin to G. verweisen to censure, OHG. firwizan, Goth. traweitan to avenge, L. videre to see. See Vision, Wit.

twitch.etymology: OE. twicchen, fr. (doubtful) AS. twiccian; akin to AS. angeltwicca a worm used for bait, literally, a hook twitcher, LG. twikken to tweak, G. zwicken. Cf. Tweak.

two.etymology: OE. two, twa, properly fem. & neut., twei, twein, tweien, properly masc. (whence E. twain), AS. twa, fem. & neut., tw, masc., t, neut.; akin to OFries. tw, masc., twa, fem. & neut., OS. tw, masc., twa, fem., tw, neut., D. twee, OHG. zw, zw, zwei, G. zwei, Icel. tveir, tvær, tvau, Sw. två, Dan. to, Goth. twai, tw, twa; Lith. du, Russ. dva, Ir. & Gael. da, W. dau, dwy, L. duo, Gr. dva. Balance, Barouche, Between, Bi-, Combine, Deuce two in cards, Double, Doubt, Dozen, Dual, Duet, Dyad, Twain, Twelve, Twenty, Twice, Twilight, Twig, Twine, n., Twist.

roots.meaning: In the composition of chemical names bi- denotes two atoms, parts, or equivalents of that constituent to the name of which it is prefixed, to one of the other component, or that such constituent is present in double the ordinary proportion; as, bichromate, bisulphide. Be- and di- are often used interchangeably.

tympan.etymology: F., fr. tympanum a kettledrum, a panel of a door. See Tympanum, and cf. Tymp.

tympanitic.etymology: L. tympaniticus one afflicted with tympanites.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

tympanum.etymology: L., a kettledrum, a drum or wheel in machines, the triangular area in a pediment, the panel of a door, Gr. Type, and cf. Timbrel.

type.etymology: F. type; cf. It. tipo, from L. typus a figure, image, a form, type, character, Gr. tup to hurt.

typhoid.etymology: Typhus + -oid: cf. F. typhoïde, Gr. Typhus.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

typhoon.etymology: Earlier tuffoon, tuffon, Pg. tufao, Ar. tufan a violent storm; probably fr. Gr. tyfw^n, tyfw^s, a violent whirlwind, that rushes upward from the earth, whirling clouds of dust (cf. Typhus); or perhaps from Chin. t'ai-fung a cyclonic wind.

typical.etymology: L. typicus, Gr. typique. See Type.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.
A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

tyrannic.etymology: L. tyrannicus, Gr. tyrannique. See Tyrant.

tyrannical.etymology: L. tyrannicus, Gr. tyrannique. See Tyrant.

tyrannicide.etymology: L. tyrannicidium the killing of a tyrant, tyrannicida the killer of a tyrant; tyrannus a tyrant + caedere to kill: cf. F. tyrannicide.

tyranny.etymology: OE. tirannye, OF. tirannie, F. tyrannie; cf. It. tirannia; Gr. tyrannis. See Tyrant.

tyro.etymology: L. tiro a newlylevied soldier, a beginner.
